item.title: Eight Nigerian soldiers killed as army vehicle hits landmine
item.description: A Nigerian army patrol vehicle hit a landmine planted by Islamic State group-aligned jihadists near the border with Cameroon, killing eight soldiers, defence sources told AFP Sunday. The attack happened in the northeastern state of Borno on Saturday, the same day the Nigerian army chief, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, was visiting the state capital, Maiduguri, over an attack on a base days earlier that killed 15 soldiers and five anti-jihadist militia members. Jihadist violence in Nigeria which erupted in 2009 has eased since its peak a decade ago, but violence has been on the rise in the last two years. In the latest attack, troops were inspecting anti-jihadist militia members who were clearing thickets along the highway outside the town of Gamboru when their vehicle rolled over the mine and exploded, killing all eight on board, the sources said. The sources blamed the attack on Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), which is active in the area. Jihadists use thickets along the highway as cover to ambush troops and motorists. “All eight soldiers in the vehicle were killed in the explosion,” which happened in Kinuba village, 25 kilometres (15.5 miles) from Gamboru, a military officer in the region said. Ibrahim Liman, an anti-jihadist militia member assisting the military against jihadists, gave the same toll. “The explosive was planted on the dusty road and remotely detonated by a detonating cord,” Liman said. A militia member supervising the thicket clearing was injured by shrapnel, said Liman. ISWAP and rival jihadist group Boko Haram have increasingly resorted to planting mines on highways against military and civilian targets. The long jihadist conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around two million from their homes in Nigeria’s northeast. The violence has spread to neighbouring Niger, Chad and Cameroon, prompting a regional military coalition to fight the militants. abu/jhb The post Eight Nigerian soldiers killed as army vehicle hits landmine appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: EU pledges €20m defence support to Nigerian military
item.description: The European Union (EU) has pledged €20 million in defence support to the Armed Forces of Nigeria (AFN) under the European Peace Facility (EPF), as Nigeria seeks to strengthen its military operations against terrorists and other security threats. The proposed assistance was discussed when the Minister of Defence, General Christopher Musa (Rtd), met with the EU Ambassador to Nigeria and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), Gautier Mignot, at Ship House in Abuja. Leah Katung-Babatunde, Special Assistant on Media to the Minister of Defence, disclosed this in a statement on Saturday. According to the statement, the meeting focused on key bilateral defence agreements and a review of security cooperation between Nigeria and the EU. Katung-Babatunde said Mignot commended Musa’s efforts to improve the country’s security situation and invited him to a meeting of defence ministers scheduled to hold in Brussels later in the year. She added that discussions also centred on arrangements for the EU’s €20 million assistance package to the Nigerian military under the EPF. The ambassador, she said, disclosed that an EU technical delegation would visit Nigeria in November to agree on the details of the proposed support. Musa thanked the EU for its continued support for Nigeria and reaffirmed President Bola Tinubu’s commitment to protecting lives and promoting national development. The minister said relative peace was gradually returning to some troubled parts of the country through the efforts of the armed forces and other security agencies. He, however, identified kidnapping along major highways and attacks on isolated communities as persistent security challenges. Musa also disclosed that Nigeria was expecting the delivery of 10 attack helicopters, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and other military equipment to strengthen security operations. On regional security, the minister identified the shrinking of the Lake Chad Basin, which supports more than 50 million people, as a factor contributing to instability in the region. He said denying terrorists access to holding areas on islands in Lake Chad remained a key operational priority for the Multinational Joint Task Force (MNJTF), which coordinates regional efforts against insurgency. On the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration (DDR) programme, Musa said the initiative would prioritise victims of the conflict, including military personnel affected by the fighting. item.title: FRSC Ogun Sector Commander, Ogunjobi, dies after brief illness
item.description: By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta The Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) has announced the death of its Ogun State Sector Commander, Corps Commander Oludare Ogunjobi, following a brief illness. The FRSC RS2.2 Ogun State Sector Command announced his death in a statement issued on Sunday, expressing sadness over the loss of the senior officer. The statement, signed by the Command’s Public Relations Officer, Chief Route Commander Afolabi Odunsi, described Ogunjobi’s death as a significant loss to the Corps and the wider road safety community. “His passing is a great loss to the Corps, his colleagues, and the entire road safety community,” the statement said. The Command said the late sector commander would be remembered for his leadership, commitment to road safety administration and dedication to the mandate of the Corps. It added that he contributed to efforts to promote safer roads, enhance public enlightenment, strengthen stakeholder engagement and improve compliance with traffic regulations. According to the statement, his commitment to these areas formed an important part of his service to the FRSC and its mission to improve road safety. The Command also extended its condolences to Ogunjobi’s family, loved ones, colleagues and associates, acknowledging the grief caused by his death. “His demise is deeply regretted, and the Command extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones, colleagues, and associates during this difficult period,” the statement added. The FRSC said details of the funeral arrangements would be communicated in due course. The statement concluded with a prayer for the repose of the deceased’s soul and strength for his family, colleagues and others affected by his passing. “May God grant his soul eternal rest and give his family, the Corps, and all those affected by his passing the strength to bear this irreparable loss,” it said. item.title: Ukraine Drone Attack Kills One, Sets Two Russian Oil Refineries Ablaze
item.description: A “massive” Ukrainian drone attack overnight killed one person, wounded five others and set two oil refineries ablaze in the Russian city of Saint Petersburg, its governor said Sunday. “One person was killed and five others hurt and hospitalised following a massive attack carried out by Ukrainian Nazi military drones,” governor Alexandre Beglov said. He added firefighters were battling blazes at the Saint Petersburg oil terminal site, also hit in June, the Ruchi oil depot and industrial warehouses in the Kolpino district south of the city. Beglov added several residential buildings had been hit, as well as two houses. “Air defence systems are in operation,” he wrote on Telegram. Smoke rises above the city following an air attack on the oil terminal in Saint Petersburg on October 18, 2026, amid the ongoing Russian-Ukrainian conflict. (Photo by AFP) City authorities said the attack also disrupted flights at Saint Petersburg’s main airport, one of the country’s busiest, which was restricting operations “for safety reasons”, Beglov said. The strikes came after Ukraine’s leader Volodymyr Zelensky said this week Kyiv would resume hitting Russian refineries, after an “energy ceasefire” announced by US President Donald Trump failed to materialise. Zelensky insisted he was standing up for his war-torn country in the face of unrelenting Russian attacks, including on energy infrastructure, as support from the United States slumped. The governor of the Leningrad region surrounding Saint Petersburg, Alexander Drozdenko, said 145 drones had been shot down and said around 20,000 people were without electricity following the drone raid. “A large-scale UAV (unmanned aerial vehicle) attack continues to be repelled,” Drozdenko wrote on Telegram. A police car is parked in front of a burning oil terminal following an air attack in Saint Petersburg on October 18, 2026, amid the ongoing Russian-Ukrainian conflict. (Photo by AFP) Saint Petersburg and the surrounding region are home to major oil infrastructure. Ukraine has specifically targeted the sector over recent months in retaliation for Russian bombings. TASS news agency said the attack was the largest on the region since the start of the war in February 2022. A June 6 attack saw 144 drones shot down, according to officials. Russia’s defence ministry said overall 1,015 Ukrainian drones were neutralised Saturday night in around 15 regions in Russia’s south and west, including the capital, Moscow. The Russian VK social network said the attack targeted one of its data centres in the region but that the site was working as normal. Trump, who has repeatedly criticised Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and oil depots, signed an executive order on Friday to waive sanctions and tariffs targeting Moscow’s energy revenues. item.title: ‘Record’ 855 People Arrested Over Paris Protest Violence – Police
item.description: Police in Paris said Sunday they had arrested a “record” 855 people over protest violence in the capital the day before, with the prosecutor’s office saying more than 500 were being held in custody. The capital, and many other French cities, on Saturday experienced clashes between police and protesters, multiple street blazes and widespread looting. Paris’s deputy mayor Lamia El Aaraje said the capital had been hit by “a level of violence that I believe we had never seen before”. French gendarmes patrol by a broken frontage windows of a shop a day after riot and looting following a nationwide protest against the “high cost of living”, in Lyon central-eastern France on October 18, 2026. (Photo by JEFF PACHOUD / AFP) The Paris prosecutor’s office said that, of those in custody, 346 were adults and 171 were minors, for a total of 517. It added that the numbers were provisional and could change. “Arrests took place throughout the night and up to 6:00 am (0400 GMT) this morning,” the office said. Most of the arrests were for receiving stolen goods, association with intent to commit violence, and vandalism, it said. item.title: I’ve been diabetic since 1996 – Actor Jide Kosoko
item.description: Veteran Nollywood actor Jide Kosoko has revealed that he has been living with diabetes since 1996, saying his years of experience with the condition have helped him understand his health better. The actor made this disclosure during a recent episode on ‘Talk to B’ Show. “I have been diabetic since 1996; I have been managing it. I understand my health better than some doctors do. Do not misquote me. I am not saying I know how to do everything, I just do not want to die,” Kosoko said. The veteran actor also spoke about his personal life, revealing that he had lost three wives, including the mother of his daughter, Bidemi Kosoko, who died during childbirth. “I lost my wife during childbirth; that’s Bidemi’s mother. I have lost three wives,” he said. Kosoko, who began his career in theatre as a child, also reflected on his longstanding contribution to the Nigerian entertainment industry. “I started theatre at age 10, in 1964, and formed my own group in 1972. I make bold to say that I am one of the pioneers of this industry,” he said. The actor also offered parenting advice, urging parents to treat their children equally and ensure that each child feels loved and valued. “Treat your children equally; let them know they’re equal in your mind,” he said. Speaking about social media, Kosoko recalled that people were initially apprehensive about the platform but noted that it had since become useful to many. “When social media was coming, we were afraid. But now we use it to our advantage. Some use it uselessly. Must you shake your bumbum and talk about jargons before you make money?” he asked. item.title: NDLEA issues public alert after intercepting woman with drugs concealed in palm oil keg
item.description: The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) has warned Nigerians against accepting parcels or luggage from other people for delivery, after its operatives discovered illicit drugs concealed in a keg of palm oil intended for shipment to Saudi Arabia. Femi Babafemi, the agency’s director of media and advocacy, issued the warning in an X post titled “Public Alert”, accompanied by a video showing NDLEA officials removing substances wrapped in polythene from a keg. Babafemi said the consignment was given to a woman travelling to Saudi Arabia, who was asked to deliver it to another person in the Middle Eastern country. According to him, the woman was intercepted by NDLEA officers at the airport, where the concealed drugs were discovered. “We’ll never be tired of repeating this warning: Never accept any parcel or luggage from anyone or on behalf of anyone no matter how close you’re!” Babafemi wrote. He warned that the woman could have faced severe consequences if the drugs had been discovered by authorities in Saudi Arabia. “She’ll have been counting her days on earth by now if this was discovered in Saudi,” he said. Babafemi urged Nigerians to exercise caution when asked to transport items for other people, regardless of their relationship with the person making the request. He advised travellers to prioritise their safety and freedom over the fear of offending friends, relatives or acquaintances who ask them to carry packages. “Choose to offend the person than go to jail. BE WISE!” he added. The NDLEA spokesperson also called on Nigerians to share the warning with their friends and family members to prevent unsuspecting travellers from becoming involved in drug trafficking. The agency has repeatedly cautioned travellers against accepting packages whose contents they cannot independently verify, as traffickers may exploit personal relationships and unsuspecting couriers to move illicit substances across borders. item.title: SERAP sues INEC over alleged ₦126bn missing electoral funds
item.description: The Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) has sued the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) over its alleged failure to account for more than ₦126.46bn appropriated for electoral operations. In a statement signed by Kolawole Oluwadare, SERAP deputy director on Sunday, the organisation is asking the Federal High Court in Abuja to compel INEC to disclose details of the expenditure, utilisation and disbursement of the funds, which were earmarked for the procurement of election materials, equipment, vehicles and other services. According to SERAP, the allegations are contained in the 2023 audited report of the Auditor-General of the Federation, published on August 7, 2026. The report covers transactions from January to December 2022, with some extending to December 31, 2023. In suit number FHC/ABJ/CS/2507/2026, filed last week, SERAP is seeking “an order of mandamus to direct and compel INEC to promptly disclose detailed information on the expenditure, utilisation and disbursement of over ₦126.46 billion appropriated for electoral operations, including the procurement of election materials, equipment, and vehicles.” The organisation is also seeking “an order of mandamus to direct and compel INEC to disclose a full financial and documentary account of the over ₦126 billion appropriated for electoral operations, including amounts released and paid, payment beneficiaries, details of contractors and their beneficial owners.” SERAP argued that the allegations raised questions about the management of public funds intended to support Nigeria’s electoral process. “Electoral resources are public resources. SERAP also cited an alleged payment of more than ₦1.05bn for Toyota Prado TXL 2021 Model vehicles. The suit stated that INEC “paid over ₦1 billion [₦1,058,925,000.00] for Toyota Prado TXL 2021 Model without advertisement, competitive bidding, bid evaluation or a BPP Certificate of No Objection.” It added that the Auditor-General feared the money “may have been lost” and that the contracts “may have been inflated.” The organisation also alleged that more than ₦3.13bn was paid to four contractors for ballot guides, sensitive materials and result sheets before the contracts were awarded. “INEC ‘paid over ₦3 billion [₦3,136,806,050.00] to four contractors for ballot guides, sensitive materials and result sheets before the contracts were awarded, with no evidence of payment.’ The Auditor-General is concerned that the money ‘may have been diverted.’ He wants the money recovered and remitted to the treasury,” the suit stated. On another transaction, SERAP alleged that INEC “paid over ₦9 billion [₦9,245,965,502.60] for 22 contracts for similar goods and services”, with the contracts “split to circumvent procurement procedures and awarded on the same day.” The Auditor-General reportedly said the money “may have been lost” and that “the payment may have been made for items not supplied.” The suit also raised concerns over payments to accounting firms, alleging that INEC “paid over ₦129 million [₦129,375,000.00] to 19 accounting firms for financial audit services without evidence of utilisation or requests and expenditure by the consultants.” It stated that the Auditor-General believed the money “may have been diverted” and wanted it recovered and remitted to the treasury. On accreditation devices, SERAP alleged that INEC “paid over ₦504 million [₦504,492,641.00] for accreditation devices without due procurement process.” The suit added that the “APG had expired before the security licence key was delivered and the software was valid for only four months, raising questions about economy and value for money.” SERAP also cited an alleged payment of more than ₦235m to contractors for sleeping mats and digital archiving, claiming that INEC “paid over ₦235 million [₦235,103,000.00] to unqualified contractors for sleeping mats and digital archiving.” The Auditor-General reportedly identified “serious concerns regarding the eligibility and capacity of the contractors” and raised concerns that the money “may have been lost.” Among its requests, SERAP wants INEC to provide documentary and physical evidence that the more than ₦112bn identified as irregularly paid was used to procure the relevant electoral materials, including details of their current location and status. “Nigerians have a right to know every public act, everything that is done in the public interest, by their public institutions including INEC,” the organisation stated. It also urged the court to direct INEC to preserve electoral equipment, materials and other public assets covered by the audit findings. “INEC should be directed to ensure that no electoral equipment, material or other public asset covered by the Auditor-General’s findings is disposed of, transferred, destroyed, written off or otherwise dealt with in a manner that could frustrate transparency and accountability,” the suit stated. SERAP further called for the publication of the names of contractors, suppliers and consultants who allegedly received the funds irregularly, as well as any public officials who authorised or facilitated the transactions or benefited from them. The organisation said Nigerians were entitled to know whether the contracted goods and services were supplied, whether payments matched the items delivered and whether contracts were deliberately split to evade procurement requirements. It also cited Section 15(5) of the Nigerian Constitution, which requires public institutions to abolish corrupt practices and abuse of power, as well as Section 13, which sets out responsibilities relating to the implementation of the Constitution’s Chapter II provisions. SERAP further referenced Nigeria’s obligations under the United Nations Convention against Corruption, Article 25 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and Article 13 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights. The organisation said the legal provisions support transparency in public financial management and citizens’ participation in public affairs. No date has been fixed for the hearing of the suit. item.title: Out-of-control truck kills 13 at Hindu festival in India
item.description: A speeding truck in India killed 13 people when it ploughed into a crowd at a Hindu festival, officials said on Sunday, with President Droupadi Murmu describing the deaths as “heartbreaking”. The heavily loaded truck reportedly lost control in the early hours of Sunday and hit devotees gathered at a temple in Gwalior, in the central state of Madhya Pradesh. The Press Trust of India (PTI) news agency cited hospital officials as saying 13 people had died. “I express my deepest condolences to the bereaved families and pray for the swift recovery of those injured,” Murmu said on social media. India, with 1.4 billion people, recorded more than 183,000 road traffic deaths in 2025, or over 500 a day, according to the roads ministry. Many are linked to inadequate road infrastructure, ill-maintained vehicles and exhausted drivers, according to official data. item.title: Accord Lagos chairman seeks clarity over Adeleke’s Tinubu campaign role
item.description: Mr Oladele Oladeji, Lagos State Chairman of Accord, has called for clarification over Gov. Ademola Adeleke’s reported appointment as coordinator of President Bola Tinubu’s 2027 presidential campaign in Osun. Oladeji said the reported appointment raised concerns about its implications for Accord’s political identity, candidates and electoral prospects. In an open letter to the party’s national leadership on Saturday, he questioned Adeleke’s political allegiance, given that he was elected governor on Accord’s platform. “Our letter was a genuine expression of concern about the implications of Governor Adeleke’s reported appointment as coordinator of President Tinubu’s 2027 presidential campaign in Osun,” he said. Oladeji said his intervention was not intended to usurp the responsibilities of the National Working Committee or any other constituted party organ. “A concerned party member does not need special authorisation to ask questions about the direction of the party to which they belong,” he said. He described his intervention as a legitimate expression of concern about the party’s future, rather than an attempt to undermine its leadership or constitutional structures. Oladeji acknowledged Adeleke’s right to make personal political decisions but argued that such choices should be assessed against the interests of Accord. He said Adeleke’s position as the party’s elected governor made his political decisions significant to its public identity, candidates and members. “Accord’s independent political direction, the electoral prospects of the party’s candidates and the party’s national ambition demand a distinct allegiance to the party’s electoral ambitions and goals,” he said. Oladeji urged Adeleke to remain committed to the electoral success of Accord candidates nationwide, noting that party members had supported his governorship election. He said political cooperation was not inherently objectionable but insisted that its terms, objectives and consequences should be clearly communicated to party members and candidates. “Our concern is whether the terms, objectives and consequences of such cooperation are sufficiently clear to members and candidates who must carry the party’s name before the electorate,” he said. Oladeji reaffirmed his position on the original letter, saying he would continue seeking clarification from the appropriate party authorities. He said his intervention aimed to promote accountability and protect the interests of Accord and its candidates, rather than provoke unnecessary disputes. He urged the party’s national leadership to clarify its political direction and explain the implications of the reported arrangement to members and the public. “We will continue to express our concerns respectfully, rely on verifiable facts and defend the right of party members to seek clarity about the future of their political platform,” he said. item.title: 2027: APC chairman predicts 70% North’s votes for Tinubu
item.description: The All Progressives Congress (APC) National Chairman, Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda, says the North will deliver more than 70 per cent of its votes to President Bola Tinubu in 2027. Yilwatda spoke on Saturday in Abuja at the opening of Arewa for Asiwaju (A4A), a political pressure group mobilising support for Tinubu and the APC. He described the 2027 presidential election as an opportunity to renew Tinubu’s mandate, citing infrastructure projects, political appointments and inclusive governance. The APC chairman expressed confidence that northern voters would support Tinubu’s re-election, arguing that the region had benefited significantly from his administration. He listed road projects across the North, including the Trans-Saharan Super Highway, covering routes from Benue through the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Akwanga, Jos, Maiduguri and Biu. “I can’t mention all of them, but President Tinubu has done wonderfully. He has covered all the geopolitical zones in the North in terms of road projects,” he said. Yilwatda said the administration was also undertaking railway and healthcare projects across the region, including health centres and free medical services for pregnant women. He identified the appointment of northerners to key political positions as another reason the region should support Tinubu’s re-election. The APC chairman urged supporters to secure votes for Tinubu at the grassroots, expressing confidence in their ability to deliver the projected 70 per cent. “Even if in our hometown alone we can win our polling units for President Tinubu, we have over 70 per cent of the vote in the North, just us alone in our polling units. “So we have no reason not to return Tinubu. His background in history, policy analysis, and public administration gave him an unusual combination of academic depth and practical statecraft. It was this reputation that brought him into the newspaper industry at a decisive moment in Nigerian media history. Transformation of the Daily Times Cole came into public prominence in 1975 when he was appointed a non-executive director of the Daily Times, representing government interests on the board. In 1976, he became Managing Director of the newspaper at a time when the institution was undergoing major political and organisational upheaval. The Daily Times was then one of the largest and most influential newspaper organisations in Africa, with numerous publications and subsidiaries, including Times Press and Niger Pack. Following the federal government’s acquisition of a controlling stake in the company, Cole’s immediate task was to restore stability, confidence, and professional harmony within the organisation. His tenure is remembered for several enduring achievements. Amongst those achievements are the fact that he rebuilt morale and strengthened the professional structure of the Daily Times after a period of crisis. He also established Nigeria’s first newspaper Editorial Board modelled on American practice, separating systematic editorial opinion-making from the traditional features-department approach. Cole brought leading intellectuals, including Dr. Stanley Macebuh, Doyin Abiola, Olu Akaraogun, Dele Giwa, and Sam Oni, into the paper’s editorial culture. He defended editorial independence, notably backing editors who resisted pressure to suppress sensitive stories. He continued the Daily Times tradition of investing in staff training and human-capital development. Under Cole, the newspaper retained its hard-hitting editorial voice while also achieving commercial success. His administration is widely credited with helping the Daily Times regain its stature as a leading African newspaper. Champion of editorial independence Perhaps Cole’s most important legacy in journalism is his defence of the newspaper as an institution of accountability. Although he entered the Daily Times as a government-appointed director, he did not behave as an instrument for muzzling the press. Instead, he protected editors and insisted that the newspaper’s primary loyalty was to its readers and to the public interest. A celebrated example involved the Sunday Times and a planned lead story on Nigeria Airways. When government officials sought to stop publication, the editor refused. Cole backed the editor, reinforcing the principle that editorial decisions should not be dictated by political convenience. He also stood with Daily Times editor Tony Momoh in the celebrated confrontation over the Senate’s attempt to summon the editor over publication of a Senate document. The episode became a landmark in the struggle for press freedom and editorial autonomy in Nigeria. Cole later became associated with The Guardian’s Editorial Board, where he continued to contribute to public debate. His influence helped make the newspaper’s editorial board one of the most respected in Nigerian journalism. Diplomatic career Cole later moved into diplomacy. He served as Nigeria’s Ambassador to Brazil from 1990 to 1993, during the administration of General Ibrahim Babangida ,retd, and was also accredited to Argentina. In later interviews, he explained that he considered it his duty to remind political leaders of their promises and obligations, even when doing so was unpopular. He argued that public officials owe the people honesty, especially on commitments that are ethical and part of their declared programmes. He subsequently served as Special Adviser on International Relations to President Olusegun Obasanjo, bringing his diplomatic experience and policy expertise back into the heart of government. item.description: Emi Martinez has undergone surgery following a head injury sustained during Chelsea’s 2-0 Premier League victory over Everton on Saturday, with the goalkeeper saying he expects to return in a few weeks. The Argentina international, 34, suffered the injury in the 67th minute at Hill Dickinson Stadium when he collided with Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite while attempting to punch an Everton free kick away from his penalty area. He promised to do inner roads and ensure demolition of buildings was not the first option at OPIC lands at Ilutuntun, Agbara and other areas. The senator pledged to strengthen agriculture and food security through diversification, improve educational standards and human capital development, and expand access to healthcare. item.description: By Kingsley Omonobi The National Security Adviser, Nuhu Ribadu, has said sustained military operations are degrading terrorist activities across Nigeria, but stressed that lasting peace requires stronger intelligence-sharing, effective border control and active community participation. Ribadu said the evolving nature of banditry and terrorism demanded a comprehensive security strategy combining military pressure with intelligence gathering, law enforcement and measures to disrupt the supply of illicit weapons to criminal groups. He spoke at the weekend through the Director of Legal Services in the Office of the National Security Adviser, Zakari Usman Mijinyawa, at a brainstorming session on insecurity organised by the Sokoto Advancement Forum in collaboration with the Centre for Peace Studies, Usmanu Danfodiyo University, Sokoto. The NSA identified Operation Fansan Yamma as a key platform for coordinating security operations across the North-West, stressing the importance of sustained military engagement in confronting armed groups and restricting their operational freedom. He said the Federal Government was also strengthening intelligence-led operations, border surveillance and coordination among security agencies to tackle the country’s complex security challenges. Ribadu disclosed that more than 19,000 illicit weapons had been destroyed since 2022 as part of efforts to reduce the availability of firearms to terrorists, bandits and other criminal networks. He said the destruction of the weapons formed part of broader efforts to weaken armed groups, while ongoing military operations sought to disrupt their movements, logistics and capacity to threaten communities. However, Ribadu warned that military action alone could not guarantee lasting peace, particularly in areas where criminal groups exploit porous borders, economic hardship and vulnerable young people for recruitment. According to him, banditry has evolved beyond cattle rustling, highway robbery and kidnapping to include attempts by armed groups to control territory, impose illegal taxes on rural communities, disrupt farming and commerce, and establish influence over local populations. item.title: Peter Obi, Obidients biggest obstacle to Igbo presidency – Segun Sowunmi
item.description: Segun Sowunmi, convener of The Alternative, has said the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, Peter Obi and his supporters, known as Obidients, are the biggest obstacles to the South-East producing Nigeria’s president. Sowunmi said the region needed to build alliances with other parts of the country and reduce political hostility if it hoped to secure the presidency in a multi-ethnic and multicultural nation. He made the remarks during an interview on the Selah Meditate Podcast , where he discussed the 2027 general election and the prospects of presidential contenders. “The biggest obstacle I see to the Igbo presidency is Peter Obi and his Obidients. Let me tell you why. Power must be negotiated,” Sowunmi said. He argued that the South-East should pursue broader political cooperation, beginning with solidarity across the South and extending to the Middle Belt and the northern region. According to him, securing the presidency requires strategic negotiations and the ability to build relationships beyond one’s immediate ethnic or political constituency. “You can’t be asking for the presidency in a multi-ethnic, multicultural country when the level of bigotry and hatred and anger is too high,” he said. Sowunmi also criticised what he described as the hostility displayed by some Obi supporters, arguing that their conduct could alienate potential allies and reinforce negative perceptions of the South-East. Asked to explain why he considered Obi and the Obidients the biggest obstacles to an Igbo presidency, he pointed to what he described as the irritation their conduct generated among other groups. “The quality of the irritation that his Obidients create all over,” he said. “A general has significant responsibility to manage his troops,” he said, adding that political leaders should ensure their supporters did not make statements that could be interpreted as tribal. Sowunmi contrasted this with Atiku Abubakar’s supporters, saying they could make provocative remarks without necessarily making them tribal. The political commentator also questioned the apparent contradiction between the economic influence of some Igbo businesspeople and the grievances expressed by them over Nigeria’s political and economic conditions. He cited their presence in markets, retail, real estate, banking and privately owned airlines, arguing that economic interests should encourage greater engagement with the country’s political system. item.title: 19 Dead, 25 Hurt In Stampede At India Religious Gathering
item.description: At least 19 people were killed and two dozen more injured Saturday in eastern India after a stampede that occurred during sudden rainfall at a Hindu religious gathering, officials and Indian media said. West Bengal’s Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari told reporters the fatalities included a seven-year-old girl, adding that 25 other people were injured outside a pavilion “in a stampede” at the Hindu festival of Durga Puja in the city of Kolkata. “Six bodies have so far been identified,” Adhikari said. A senior police official at the scene told AFP an announcement caused “commotion” after it started raining at night and the “crowd waiting outside the pandal (pavilion) was pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede.” Afterwards, medics were seen moving injured people on stretchers, including a police officer, into a local hospital. Several relatives of victims cried and held one another as they mourned the loss of loved ones. Medical workers move an injured police officer on a stretcher, following the Durga Puja Pandal stampede, in front of the emergency building of Calcutta Medical College and Hospital in Kolkata on October 16, 2026. Photo by STRINGER / AFP Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed the tragedy in a short statement on Facebook. “The stampede in Kolkata is saddening. Condolences to the bereaved families. Wishing the injured a speedy recovery,” he wrote. “The West Bengal Government is providing all possible help to the affected families.” Adhikari originally announced 17 fatalities. The Press Trust of India (PTI) reported the death toll rose by two to 19, quoting Adhikari in a later statement. Nine dead bodies have been released to their families, the PTI reported. It also said police have taken the closed circuit footage of the festival and authorities would initiate action against those seen on CCTV who appeared to fail in their responsibility for crowd control. Videos shot before the stampede appeared to show large crowds of people waiting to enter the pavilion, in an area with narrow lanes that allow only a few people to walk in at a time, according to Indian Express. Deadly crowd incidents are a frequent occurrence at Indian mass events, such as religious festivals, due to poor management and safety lapses. Last year, a stampede at India’s Kumbh Mela religious fair killed 30 people and injured several others, and 11 fans were crushed to death in Bengaluru during celebrations for the local cricket team’s first Indian Premier League title. The same year, 36 people were killed after a stampede broke out at a campaign rally of a popular actor-turned-politician in southern Tamil Nadu state. In 2024, 121 people were killed in northern Uttar Pradesh state during a Hindu religious gathering. item.description: The Federal Government has warned that a return to the fuel subsidy can trigger capital flight, put pressure on the naira, and undermine the gains of its economic reforms. The warning came at a media briefing in Bangkok, Thailand, at the conclusion of the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings. The Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele; the Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria, Olayemi Cardoso; and the Minister of Budget and Economic Planning, Atiku Bagudu, addressed Nigeria’s economic outlook following the conclusion of the meeting. Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy Taiwo Oyedele said on October 8, 2026, that FG’s 30-day fuel reduction is not a return of the subsidy. The finance minister said investors have repeatedly sought assurances that the government will not reverse the removal of fuel subsidy or the unification of exchange rates, particularly as the country approaches another election cycle. Oyedele argued that any signal of a possible return to subsidies could prompt investors to withdraw their capital, putting pressure on the foreign exchange market and the naira. The Minister of Finance and the Central Bank Governor arrive for the final briefing by the Nigerian delegation to the 2026 IMF-World Bank Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. After five days of deliberations, the delegation highlighted some of the key takeaways from the event, especially as they impact the administration’s economic policies. ﻿ It clarified the decision to discount the retail price of Premium Motor Spirit (PMS). The delegation also announced the Federal Government’s seven per cent economic growth target. In his remarks, the Minister of Budget and Economic Planning emphasised the need for fiscal and monetary authorities to work together to sustain the gains of the reforms. Debt, climate, AI, and inequality topped the agenda at the World Bank-IMF meeting attended by Nigeria and 190 other countries in Thailand. At the meeting, Nigeria called for comprehensive reforms of the IMF and the World Bank to give developing economies a strong voice in global financial decisions, improve access to financing and strengthen their capacity to withstand economic shocks. While presenting the Group of Twenty-Four (G-24) 2026 annual meeting communiqué in Bangkok, Thailand, on the sidelines of the World Bank/IMF Annual Meetings, Oyedele said geopolitical conflicts, trade uncertainties, volatile commodity prices and climate shocks are threatening global economic growth. According to him, the challenges disproportionately affect emerging markets and developing economies, undermining efforts to create jobs and achieve inclusive transformation. Africa and development: Debt pressures threaten investment and jobs A file photo of the World Bank headquarters in Washington, DC What happened: Reuters reported Saturday that developing countries’ external debt has reached approximately $12.3 trillion, while official development assistance fell 23 per cent in 2025. World Bank President Ajay Banga is advocating greater mobilisation of private capital as governments face growing pressure to finance infrastructure and employment. Why it matters: Debt servicing is competing with spending on electricity, education, healthcare and transport across developing economies. Business opportunities and risks: Development-finance guarantees, blended finance and public-private partnerships may become increasingly important for African infrastructure. However, high borrowing costs make poorly structured projects particularly vulnerable. Technology and AI: Industry leaders warn that regulation is lagging innovation Artificial Intelligence What happened: Speaking at the IMF–World Bank meetings, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark argued that rapid improvements in artificial intelligence could transform productivity and economic growth. He also warned that governments may be running out of time to establish effective safeguards against cybersecurity threats, biological misuse, and other risks. His company’s very large estimates of potential economic gains remain projections, not independently established outcomes. Why it matters: AI is becoming a major economic-policy issue, not merely a technology-industry concern. Media and business implications: Broadcasters face two parallel opportunities: using AI to improve production and distribution, and negotiating fair compensation when technology platforms use original journalism. Watch next: International AI regulation, news-content licensing agreements, enterprise adoption and whether investment produces measurable productivity gains. Saturday Evening’s Strategic Takeaway The clearest change since the morning briefing is the government’s renewed commitment to maintaining market-oriented economic reforms despite pressure over fuel prices. The most important developing domestic issue is security ahead of the elections. Military deployments and operational directives now need to translate into verifiable results For broadcasting and digital investment, the emerging international debate over AI regulation, intellectual property and financing remains particularly significant.
